cases.title: Same pawn move, different central responsibility
cases.comparePrompt: What central pawn is each ...f5 advance challenging, and which new weaknesses might matter? Do not infer the same evaluation just because the notation matches.
cases.model: In Steinitz–Sellman the French center features White's advanced e5 pawn; Black's ...f5 fixes a direct kingside confrontation while White replies Rc1 and Black continues ...Bb7. In Tarrasch–Von Scheve, ...f5 appears after a different Queen's Gambit pawn structure and White answers Bd6, then Black plays ...Re8. The pawn move's meaning depends on the location of the opposing pawn chain, the kings and the minor pieces—not the word 'break' alone.
cases.resistancePrompt: If Black expects ...f5 to solve both centers automatically, which concrete white response in each recorded sequence disproves that shortcut?
cases.transferPrompt: Against an alternative legal White reply, compare Black's e6-pawn, control of e5 and king exposure before advocating ...f5 again.
cases.misconception: Treating identical SAN as identical strategic instruction. Repair: name the pawn chain and the first recorded reply in both games, then identify one square newly controlled and one concession.
hints: Locate the side to move, every pawn that controls the central four squares, and the two kings before naming a plan.
